raw_text:
The coronary slow flow phenomenon (CSFP) is an angiographic entity characterized by delayed distal opacification of one or more epicardial coronary arteries despite absent or non-flow-limiting stenosis. First described by Tambe and colleagues in 1972 [1], CSFP has moved from being an angiographic curiosity to a clinically relevant form—or marker—of coronary vascular dysfunction. Objective assessment is usually by the thrombolysis in myocardial infarction frame count (TFC), particularly the corrected TFC for the left anterior descending artery, with values >27 frames often used to define slow flow [2]. Contemporary definitions emphasize exclusion of secondary causes, including epicardial spasm, ectasia, embolism, no-reflow after intervention, severe valvular disease, cardiomyopathy and significant epicardial coronary artery disease [3,4].

Reported prevalence varies with case definition and referral population, ranging from about 1% to 7% among patients undergoing coronary angiography, and the syndrome is enriched among men, smokers, patients with higher body mass index, low high-density lipoprotein cholesterol and other cardiometabolic risk factors [5-10]. Clinically, CSFP commonly presents with recurrent rest angina or acute coronary syndrome–like symptoms, often leading to repeat emergency visits despite “normal” or near-normal angiography [3,7,10,11]. Although historically considered benign, persistent symptoms, impaired quality of life, ischemic electrocardiographic changes and occasional ventricular arrhythmias argue against dismissing the finding [5-8].

Pathophysiology is heterogeneous. Early biopsy data demonstrated small-vessel structural abnormalities, including arteriolar wall thickening and luminal narrowing, supporting a microvascular substrate [9]. Physiological studies have shown increased resting microvascular resistance, abnormal coronary sinus metabolic findings and, in some cohorts, reduced coronary flow reserve [10,11]. Endothelial dysfunction is a recurring theme: patients with CSFP show impaired brachial flow-mediated dilation, reduced nitric oxide bioavailability and associations with homocysteine-related oxidative stress [12-14]. Low-grade inflammation may also contribute, with studies reporting higher high-sensitivity C-reactive protein and interleukin-6 concentrations proportional to TFC [15,16]. Another proposed mechanism is diffuse, angiographically occult atherosclerosis: intravascular ultrasound and fractional flow reserve studies have identified intimal thickening, calcification and diffuse epicardial resistance even when angiography appears normal [17,18]. Platelet activation and blood rheology may amplify microvascular resistance, as suggested by associations between mean platelet volume and the presence or extent of CSFP [23].

The relationship between CSFP and coronary microvascular dysfunction (CMD) remains unsettled. CSFP has often been interpreted as a visual surrogate of CMD, yet studies conflict: some show impaired coronary flow reserve [11], whereas others demonstrate preserved hyperemic reserve despite elevated resting resistance [10]. More recent invasive and imaging work suggests that slow angiographic transit does not reliably diagnose endothelium-dependent or endothelium-independent CMD in all patients with angina and unobstructed coronary arteries [21,22]. Thus, CSFP should be regarded as a specific angiographic phenotype that overlaps with, but is not synonymous with, CMD.

Management is not standardized and evidence is limited by small, single-center trials. Initial care should confirm the diagnosis, exclude mimics, quantify TFC, assess ischemic burden when appropriate and treat cardiovascular risk factors aggressively. Statins may improve endothelial function and coronary flow in selected patients [24]. Nebivolol has been associated with improved endothelial indices and exercise parameters [25]. Calcium-channel blockade has the strongest mechanistic rationale: diltiazem improved coronary flow and angina in a randomized trial [26], mibefradil reduced angina and improved angiographic flow before its market withdrawal [27], and intracoronary nicardipine can acutely reverse spontaneous slow flow, implicating microvascular spasm [28]. Dipyridamole and nicorandil have shown favorable effects on ventricular functional measures and symptoms in small studies [29,30]. Nitrates are inconsistently helpful and may be less effective when resistance is predominantly microvascular rather than epicardial.

In summary, CSFP is a reproducible angiographic syndrome with recurrent angina, variable ischemic expression and multifactorial biology involving microvascular dysfunction, endothelial impairment, inflammation, occult atherosclerosis and platelet activation. Future studies should standardize diagnostic thresholds, integrate invasive coronary function testing, and evaluate phenotype-guided therapy in adequately powered randomized trials.
